newsitem.title: USA: U.S. says EU backing away from technology accord.
newsitem.headline: U.S. says EU backing away from technology accord.

text.p: Acting U.S. Trade Representative Charlene Barshefsky said Friday the European Union appears to be backing away from its previous support for a global agreement to cut duties on information technology.
"Europe seems to be backing away now, which would be greatly disappointing," Barshefsky told reporters.

U.S. trade officials had hoped that a global agreement to end tariffs on a variety of information technology products could be announced at the World Trade Organisation ministerial meeting to be held in mid-December in Singapore.
But Barshefsky said that would be impossible without Europe signing on to the pact.

"It is impossible to do a multilateral (Information Technology Agreement) without Europe," Barshefsky told a news conference. "We will not let Europe (take a) free ride off of tariff reductions on this broad array of products. Europe needs to be a part of this."

The agreement would cover a wide range of products, including semiconductors, computer hardware and software, and telephone equipment. Barshefsky said a technology accord would be an important demonstration of the WTO's ability to deal with market-opening issues on a continuing basis.
"Europe needs to demonstrate leadership here," Barshefsky said. "This is not the time for Europe to be backing away from the multilateral process and backing away from the trans-Atlantic dialogue."

The trans-Atlantic dialogue involves a group of business leaders from both Europe and North America working to find ways to lower barriers, harmonise standards and reduce the cost of trade. A global agreement eliminating tariffs on information technologies was one of the recommendations made by that group, Barshefsky said.

The idea of an information technology agreement was endorsed this spring at a meeting in Japan of the trade ministers of the European Union, Canada, United States and Japan. Barshefsky said the four ministers will take up the issue again next week when they meet in Seattle.

Privately, U.S. and industry officials say they are unsure of Europe's motives in moving away from the agreement, which is winning support in Asia. They suggested it might be a bargaining position or reflect a lack of uniform support within the European Union.
Part of the problem, they said, is that Europe has relatively high tariffs on those products, while the United States and Japan have very low, or in some cases, no import duties on them.
Barshefsky said the information technology agreement is one of two areas where the WTO could demonstrate it can lower trade barriers and open new markets.

She said the second area is government procurement and U.S. efforts to get an interim global agreement on opening up the purchasing process to more public scrutiny. Washington sees this as a way of reducing corruption and bribery, a major problem for U.S. corporations, which are forbidden by U.S. law from paying bribes to win contracts.
